item.title: Addressing medical issues in prisons. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The revelation that 54 prisons across Bangladesh lack ambulances is nothing short of shocking.
At a time when our country should be trying to modernize its justice and correctional systems, the fact that thousands of inmates have no access to emergency transport exposes a severe and dangerous gap in basic state responsibility and an utter disregard for humanity.
Prisons house some of the most vulnerable people - individuals with limited access to healthcare, often living in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions, and frequently suffering from chronic illnesses.
When medical emergencies occur, delays can and have been fatal with the lack of timely care. This is unacceptable, and calls for a very basic understanding that inmates in prison are human beings as well and deserve to be treated as such.
We have, at this point, a correctional system that violates among the most fundamental principles of human rights -- the right to life and medical treatment.
The state simply cannot ignore this issue any longer. Allocating ambulances to every prison should not be seen as a luxury but rather a minimum requirement.
However, the solution must go beyond vehicles. Bangladesh needs a comprehensive overhaul of prison healthcare, including trained medical staff, functioning clinics, emergency equipment, and clear protocols for rapid response.
Prisoners may be serving sentences, but they remain under the care of the state. Their health and safety should be non‑negotiable. A correctional system that cannot care for those within it is not one that can be looked at in a positive light.
This is a state of affairs that demands immediate correction. Every prison should have the bare minimum capacity to protect the lives of those in its custody.

item.title: Creating a reliable railway system. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The announcement of more trains on the Dhaka-Cox’s Bazar route to address demand is undeniably positive.
Rail connectivity to Cox’s Bazar has already transformed travel for millions, and adding another pair of trains will ease pressure on existing services, improve accessibility, and strengthen economic links between the capital and our most significant tourism hub.
With that said, this development should be seen as part of a much larger national need: We have long needed to invest far more - and far more consistently - in our rail network.
For decades, rail has been treated as a secondary mode of transport, overshadowed by highways and short‑term road expansion. The result is visible everywhere: Congested highways, unsafe long‑distance bus travel, rising transport emissions, and logistics bottlenecks that have slowed down our economy.
Rail, by contrast, is safer, cleaner, more affordable, and far more efficient for both passengers and freight.
The new Dhaka-Cox’s Bazar train pair is a step in the right direction, but we must see far more. We need a rail‑first development strategy that expands the capacity of our railways.
As such, we expect the same urgency across all rail routes to all divisions. Freight corridors too must be strengthened so industries can move goods without relying solely on trucks. And regional links - including potential future connections with India, Nepal, and Bhutan - should be part of long‑term planning.
Our ever-growing population and rising urbanization demand a transport system that can move people and goods reliably. Bangladesh has already invested heavily in megaprojects, sometimes unwisely. Now it must invest in the everyday infrastructure that keeps a country moving.
The real goal should be clear: A modern, extensive, and reliable rail network that serves the entire nation.

item.title: The battle between equity and efficiency. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Sometimes giving something away -- even, paying people to take something away -- makes a profit for the rest of us. This is obvious when we think about it. We happily pay people to take our rubbish away. When we don't just throw it in the street that is. The whole idea of a sewage system is that we're paying someone to take our rubbish away and we're better off for doing so.
How far that idea should be taken is the issue here.
We hear that 15 to 20% of the space of Chittagong port area is taken up by shipping containers that have been there for years. Near 10,000 containers in fact. Something needs to be done about this.
Chittagong is, to put this very gently, not known as the most efficient nor speedy nor even useful port globally. Being able to use more of the space to actually ship goods rather than store them would be a good idea.
Further, a more efficient Chittagong port would benefit all. Exports leave faster and sooner, imports arrive ditto, and the costs of trade decline to all our benefit.
So, get rid of those containers that have been there for years. At which point the port authorities say they do. They run an auction process and this has rules and takes time. So much time that the pile never diminishes -- the number of new containers being abandoned roughly matches the rate at which the old are cleared.
What we're facing here is our old battle between equity and efficiency. We can have a system that's really, thoroughly, fair, or a system that is brutal but works quickly.
Good policy is making sure we've the right balance of those two in any particular action.
Say, to change the subject here, we're going to require higher standards of proof in a court case where the man might get hanged than we are in one where he has to repay a Tk1,000 fine. We're willing to accept a certain amount more of getting it wrong in the second than we are the first.
This calculation, this veering of the system toward fair and to it being effective, changes depending upon what we are talking about. Here, the benefit is making the port itself more efficient to the benefit of us all. Only a small benefit for nearly 180 million people is a lot.
The loss to those 10,000 people of the auction of their container might be quite large but when added up, much less than the benefit to the rest of us.
So, be brutal about the auctions. Forget having detailed rules about this and that and telling everyone what's in the containers and everything. We even have a legal reason to confiscate those containers -- demurrage. It's an odd word but well known in trade.
If something gets stuck at a port then you've got to pay for that storage at the port. After some period of time, the demurrage charges are more than the value of the container so it all belongs to the port.
This is normal and a standard part of international trade. So, just sell off those abandoned containers for whatever. Any amount because we free up the space at the port to all our benefit by doing so.
We could even do what the Americans do. When people abandon their belongings in a storage unit, they get auctioned off. Sight unseen -- no one knows what's in there, the owners simply have not paid their bills so, on the appointed day, a couple of dozen people turn up and bid for the lot. They even make TV shows about it ( Auction Hunters and Storage Hunters are two I know about).
This balance between fair and efficient is one we face many times in the economy. Sometimes, we need to move further to one or the other.
Chittagong port is so important to the Bangladeshi economy that more efficiency is what we require here. We want the space more than we want to be fair about this.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.

item.title: Social protection needs smarter reforms. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh's social protection system has been one of the country's quiet success stories. Over the past several decades, it has helped millions of poor and vulnerable households cope with poverty, natural disasters, food insecurity, and economic shocks.
The government now spends more than Tk 120,000 crore annually on social protection -- one of the largest components of public expenditure. This sustained investment reflects a strong national commitment to inclusive development and has contributed significantly to Bangladesh's remarkable progress in poverty reduction.
Yet, despite this impressive expansion, an uncomfortable question remains: Are we getting the maximum return from this investment?
The answer is mixed. While Bangladesh spends substantially on social protection, the system remains fragmented; many benefits are too small to make a meaningful difference, and targeting errors continue to prevent support from reaching those who need it most.
As Bangladesh prepares for the next stage of development amid rising living costs, climate change, and slowing economic growth, improving the quality of social protection has become just as important as expanding its budget.
The challenge today is not simply to spend more. It is to spend smarter.
One of the biggest weaknesses of Bangladesh's social protection system is how resources are allocated. A significant share of reported social protection expenditure goes toward pensions for government employees and other expenditures that do not primarily target poor or vulnerable households.
While these expenditures serve legitimate public purposes, they should not be mistaken for poverty-focused social assistance. As a result, headline budget figures often overstate the amount of public resources that directly support the poorest citizens.
Fragmentation is another major concern. Bangladesh currently operates around 90 social protection programs administered by 25 ministries and agencies. Over time, new programs have been introduced to address emerging priorities, but many overlap in objectives and administration.
This fragmentation increases administrative costs, weakens coordination, and makes it difficult to ensure consistency in beneficiary selection and service delivery. Meanwhile, public resources are concentrated in a handful of programs, leaving many others underfunded and unable to provide adequate support.
Benefit adequacy also deserves urgent attention. Many cash transfer programs have failed to keep pace with inflation. Monthly allowances that may have been meaningful several years ago now cover only a small share of household needs.
For many beneficiaries, transfers account for only a tiny proportion of household income and provide limited protection against rising food prices or unexpected shocks.
Expanding coverage is important, but expanding coverage without ensuring adequate benefit levels risks spreading resources too thinly to make a lasting difference.
Perhaps the most critical issue is targeting. Every social protection system faces two risks: Excluding households that genuinely need assistance and including households that are relatively better off.
Bangladesh is no exception. Despite improvements in program administration, significant inclusion and exclusion errors remain. Improving targeting is therefore one of the most cost-effective ways to enhance the impact of existing public spending without necessarily increasing the overall budget.
The government's recent introduction of the Family Card Program marks an important milestone in this regard. By using Proxy Means Testing (PMT) and digital government-to-person payment systems, the program aims to improve transparency and reduce leakages.
It has the potential to become the country's most significant social protection reform since the National Social Security Strategy (NSSS) was adopted in 2015.
However, international experience suggests that no single targeting method is perfect. PMT is a useful tool, but it cannot fully capture the complex and dynamic nature of poverty.
Household circumstances change frequently, and statistical models inevitably make errors. For this reason, Bangladesh should adopt a hybrid targeting approach that combines PMT with community validation and evidence-based categorical indicators such as age, disability, occupation, housing conditions, and other easily verifiable characteristics associated with poverty.
Such an approach would improve both fairness and accuracy while strengthening public confidence in the system.
Evidence also shows that some programs consistently perform better than others. Rather than creating new schemes, policy-makers should focus on strengthening programs that have demonstrated strong targeting performance and positive impacts, including the Vulnerable Group Development (VGD) program, Mother and Child Benefit program, Old age allowance, disability allowances, and allowances for widowed and deserted women.
Increasing benefit levels, expanding coverage, improving digital payments, and regularly adjusting cash transfers for inflation would significantly enhance their effectiveness.
Bangladesh must also pay greater attention to urban poverty. Rapid urbanization has transformed the country's poverty landscape, yet social protection remains disproportionately focused on rural areas.
Low-income urban households often face insecure employment, high living costs, and limited access to formal safety nets.
Expanding successful programs such as the Open Market Sales (OMS) program, introducing labour-intensive urban public works, and gradually extending the Family Card program to urban poor households would help address this growing gap.
Looking ahead, social protection should evolve beyond providing temporary relief. The objective should be to help households build resilience and eventually graduate from poverty.
International and domestic evidence suggests that transfers become far more effective when combined with complementary interventions such as nutrition education, livelihood training, financial inclusion, and access to healthcare.
Such integrated approaches not only reduce immediate hardship but also strengthen households' capacity to withstand future shocks and improve their long-term earning potential.
Health protection deserves particular attention. Medical expenses remain one of the leading causes of financial distress among poor households in Bangladesh. A serious illness can quickly erase years of progress and push vulnerable families back into poverty.
Piloting targeted health insurance and expanding health voucher programs would strengthen the country's social protection architecture while improving access to essential healthcare for low-income households.
Bangladesh has already laid a strong foundation. The National Social Security Strategy (NSSS) provides a clear policy framework, and the Family Card program offers an opportunity to modernise beneficiary identification and program delivery.
The next phase of reform should focus on improving the quality of spending rather than simply increasing its quantity. Better targeting, stronger coordination, adequate benefits, digital delivery systems, transparent grievance mechanisms, and regular impact evaluations should become the pillars of a modern social protection system.
Bangladesh's ambition to become an upper-middle-income country cannot be achieved through economic growth alone. Growth must be accompanied by a social protection system that is efficient, equitable, transparent, and capable of protecting citizens against increasingly complex economic, health, and climate-related risks.
Smarter spending -- not simply higher spending -- should therefore guide the next generation of social protection reforms. If public resources can be directed more effectively toward those who need them most, Bangladesh will not only reduce poverty more rapidly but also build a more resilient and inclusive society for decades to come.
Akhter U Ahmed is an Emeritus Research Fellow at the International Food Policy Research Institute (IFPRI), Washington DC, USA. Md Sadat Anowar is a Research Analyst at the IFPRI-Bangladesh country office.

US to make visa bond programme permanent for people from dozens of countries. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The US State Department will make permanent a visa bond programme that could require applicants from 50 countries, mostly from Africa, to post bonds of up to $20,000 when seeking US visas, according to a federal notice posted online on Friday.

The Federal Register notice applies to B1 and B2 visas, which are issued for business and tourism travel.

“Consular officers may require covered nonimmigrant visa applicants to post a bond of up to $20,000 as a condition of visa issuance, as determined by the consular officers,” the notice said.

“The 2025 visa bond pilot, which provided a framework for the Department of State, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of the Treasury to assess the feasibility of administering a visa bond programme, has provided sufficient data to suggest that a visa bond programme is an effective tool for enforcing compliance among bonded visa holders.”

In the pilot programme, consular officers could require bonds of $5,000, $10,000 or up to $15,000. The final rule eliminates the $5,000 option and raises the maximum bond to $20,000.

The final rule goes into effect on August 3 when it is scheduled for publication in the Federal Register. In the list of 50 countries for whose citizens this programme applies, 30 are from Africa.

US officials say the policy is intended to reduce visa overstays. Immigration advocates argue it will deter legitimate travel to the United States.

Rights advocates say President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown violates free speech and due process, while creating an unsafe environment for ethnic minorities and encouraging racial profiling. Trump has defended the measures as necessary to bolster national security.

While Trump says he wants to curb illegal immigration, his administration has made legal immigration more difficult, for example, by imposing new and expensive fees for applicants of certain visas and by enforcing social media vetting for applicants and immigrants already in the country.

Earlier in May, the State Department identified nationals from the following 50 countries as being required to post visa bonds: Algeria, Angola, Antigua and Barbuda, Bangladesh, Benin, Bhutan, Botswana, Burundi, Cabo Verde, Cambodia, Central African Republic, Cote D’Ivoire, Cuba, Djibouti, Dominica, Ethiopia, Fiji, Gabon, The Gambia, Georgia, Grenada, Guinea, Guinea-Bissau, Kyrgyz Republic, Lesotho, Malawi, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mongolia, Mozambique, Namibia, Nepal, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Papua New Guinea, Sao Tome and Principe, Senegal, Seychelles, Tajikistan, Tanzania, Togo, Tonga, Tunisia, Turkmenistan, Tuvalu, Uganda, Vanuatu, Venezuela, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

item.title: PPP, PML-N continue war of words on eve of Muzaffarabad elections. [ dawn ]
item.description:
The PPP and the PML-N continued lambasting each other on Saturday, extending their rhetoric from the ongoing elections in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK) to the other party’s previous tenures in power.

The PPP and the PML-N — coalition partners in the Centre — have been engaged in a war of words since the PML-N emerged as the winner in the elections in AJK’s Mirpur division. The PPP has accused the PML-N of rigging in Mirpur and demanded re-polling.

The political temperatures remain heated as the second phase of AJK elections is set to be held tomorrow in nine constituencies of Muzaffarabad division. The third phase is scheduled for August 10 in all 12 refugee constituencies, and 11 constituencies of Poonch division.

In the latest exchange, PML-N senior leader Rana Sanaullah questioned the legitimacy of President Asif Ali Zardari’s role as he responded to PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s allegations of rigging in the 2024 general elections.

“If you call the votes secured by the prime minister votes of Forms-47, then on what forms has the president gotten votes on?” Sanaullah said.

On Wednesday, Bilawal had taken a direct jibe at Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, saying: “If someone is sitting on the PM’s seat, or someone is sitting on the CM’s position today, even a child knows that it is not because of the people’s votes or your performance but because of Form-47.”

Sanaullah, also the prime minister’s aide on political affairs and a federal minister, was addressing a gathering in Jhelum Valley alongside Kashmir Affairs Minister Amir Muqam.

Sanaullah further said: “If you say to Mian Nawaz Sharif that he became the prime minister for the first time or every time through rigging, […] then remember, it is also discussed here that someone also became the prime minister for the first time after breaking apart the country.”

He was referring to PPP founder Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, who became the president of Pakistan in December 1971 after the secession of Bangladesh (then-East Pakistan) following the 1970 elections.

In August 1973, Bhutto took the oath as the prime minister in 1973 under the new Constitution.

Sanaullah also took a jibe at Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, whose recent remarks have sparked a fresh debate in political circles on the matter of creating new provinces.

Calling Naqvi a “blessed one” of President Zardari, the PML-N leader said the interior minister had “made the [political] journey of 30 years in three-and-a-half years”.

“You began from where and have now reached where, and now you realise that this system is completely dysfunctional.”

In his speech, Muqam criticised the PPP’s governance in Sindh, saying that no performance of the party could be seen.

He also said the Benazir Income Support Programme (BISP) — a scheme that the PPP often takes credit for launching — was not “anyone’s personal programme but the government’s”.

Earlier on Saturday, PPP leader Saeed Ghani alleged that the PML-N had never won a general election without rigging.

This followed a press briefing by Punjab’s education and sports ministers, where they said that the chief ministers of Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa had nothing to show for their performance.

PML-N never won an election without rigging: Ghani

Addressing a press conference in Karachi, Ghani said, “The PPP did not secure power through rigging in any of the elections held till today.

“On the other hand, however many times the PML-N has secured power, it has not been without rigging.”

Ghani, also the Sindh labour minister, made the allegation as he responded to a PML-N member calling on the PPP to not “give lectures on democracy”.

“If you do not want to give the PPP the right to speak on democracy, then will you give it to Gen Musharraf or Gen Zia, or the leaders created by them?” he quipped, referring to the two former military dictators.

The PPP leader said he “did count the 1985 election”, alleging that PML-N supremo and ex-premier Nawaz Sharif “conspired” against ex-prime minister Mohammad Khan Junejo.

He further claimed that his party “became a target of rigging” in the 1988 and 1990 elections, which resulted in the PML-N winning. He went on to allege that the PPP was again “controlled and prevented from forming a government in Punjab” in 1993.

Ghani alleged that the PPP was restricted to “16-17 seats” in the 1997 general elections, when Nawaz’s PML-N again formed the government.

He contended that although the PPP secured power in 2008, the “PML-N was made to win seats, especially in Punjab, through rigging during Musharraf’s tenure”.

Ghani claimed that the PML-N was “made to win” the 2013 elections as well.

“Then the elections in 2024 [took place]. No matter how many times they say, everyone, even children, know that the PML-N was badly defeated in the elections,” he asserted.

The PPP leader alleged that Nawaz, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz “lost their own seats and then blame us”.

Ghani made the remarks after explaining the rationale for his party’s stances on new provinces in Sindh and Punjab, stressing that it was based on the wishes of the people.

He emphasised that the Constitution required any such move to be made through the elected representatives in the provincial assembly concerned.

He noted that the “people of Sindh, its representatives and its assembly say there is no need for further provinces in Sindh”.

On the other hand, Ghani pointed out, the Punjab Assembly and the Senate had passed resolutions over a decade ago calling for two new provinces in Punjab.

“If the people and the elected representatives of Sindh say that there is no need for any new province in Sindh, then no one in Punjab has the right to say whether there should be a new province in Sindh or not,” Ghani asserted.

He went on to stress that the PPP advocated for more provinces in Punjab as the “people of Punjab and their elected representatives” desired that.

The PPP leader emphasised that his party “represented” the citizens of each of the provinces when taking a stance for Sindh and Punjab.

At the outset of his press conference, Ghani also took exception to comments made by “two ministers”, saying it seemed that they “did not know anything about Sindh”.

“They are restricted within a circle called Maryam Nawaz. They only see and say what she tells them, shows them and explains to them,” he said in an apparent reference to the Punjab ministers.
